title: SAT Math
blurb: Topic-focused practice across the four Digital SAT domains — Algebra, Advanced Math, Problem-Solving & Data Analysis, and Geometry & Trigonometry — at the exam's three difficulty tiers.

units.title: Algebra
units.blurb: Linear equations and inequalities, systems, and linear models — about a third of every SAT Math section.

units.title: Advanced Math
units.blurb: Quadratics, exponents, function notation and exponential growth — the section that separates 600s from 700s.

units.title: Problem-Solving & Data Analysis
units.blurb: Percents, ratios, rates, means and probability — every question is a real-world sentence hiding one computation.

units.title: Geometry & Trigonometry
units.blurb: Angles, areas, the Pythagorean theorem, circles and right-triangle trig — the domain with the shortest formulas and the most traps.

forms.title: Solving linear equations
forms.skill: Distribute, collect, divide — with the signs intact.

forms.skill: In C(x) = mx + b, m is the per-unit rate and b the one-time part.

variants.statement: A plumber charges $C(x) = 25x + 20$ dollars for a job that takes $x$ hours. What is the best interpretation of the number $25$ in this context?
options: Each additional hour of work adds 25 dollars to the total charge.
The one-time fee for the service call is 25 dollars.
The total charge for a one-hour job is 25 dollars.
Each additional hour of work adds 20 dollars to the total charge.
variants.explanation: In $C(x) = 25x + 20$ the coefficient of $x$ is the rate of change: one more hour raises the charge by $25$ dollars. The constant $20$ is the one-time fee, and a one-hour job costs $45$, not $25$.

forms.title: Linear functions from two values
forms.skill: Two values fix a linear function; the slope carries you to any third.

variants.statement: The function $f$ is linear, $f(-2) = -5$, and $f(0) = -11$. What is the value of $f(2)$?
variants.explanation: The slope is $\dfrac{-11 - (-5)}{0 - (-2)} = -3$, so each step of $1$ in the input adds $-3$. From $f(0) = -11$, stepping to $2$ gives $f(2) = -11 + -3 \cdot 2 = -17$.

variants.statement: The function $f$ is linear, $f(-2) = 0$, and $f(0) = -6$. What is the value of $f(2)$?
variants.explanation: The slope is $\dfrac{-6 - (0)}{0 - (-2)} = -3$, so each step of $1$ in the input adds $-3$. From $f(0) = -6$, stepping to $2$ gives $f(2) = -6 + -3 \cdot 2 = -12$.

forms.title: Exponent rules
forms.skill: Multiply inside: add. Power: multiply. Divide: subtract.

variants.statement: If $\dfrac{(x^{1} \cdot x^{1})^{3}}{x^{1}} = x^{n}$ for all $x \ne 0$, what is the value of $n$?
variants.explanation: Inside the parentheses the exponents ADD: $x^{2}$. The power multiplies: $x^{6}$. Division subtracts: $n = 6 - 1 = 5$. Multiplying $1 \cdot 1$ instead of adding is the standard slip.

variants.statement: If $\dfrac{(x^{1} \cdot x^{1})^{3}}{x^{2}} = x^{n}$ for all $x \ne 0$, what is the value of $n$?
variants.explanation: Inside the parentheses the exponents ADD: $x^{2}$. The power multiplies: $x^{6}$. Division subtracts: $n = 6 - 2 = 4$. Multiplying $1 \cdot 1$ instead of adding is the standard slip.

forms.title: Evaluating functions
forms.skill: Substitute with parentheses — (-3)^2 is 9, and the middle term keeps its sign.

variants.statement: If $f(x) = x^2 - 5x - 4$, what is the value of $f(-3)$?
variants.explanation: $f(-3) = 1(-3)^2 - 5 \cdot -3 - 4 = 9 + 15 - 4 = 20$. The sign of the middle term is where credit is usually lost.

variants.statement: If $f(x) = x^2 - 5x - 4$, what is the value of $f(3)$?
variants.explanation: $f(3) = 1(3)^2 - 5 \cdot 3 - 4 = 9 - 15 - 4 = -10$. The sign of the middle term is where credit is usually lost.

variants.statement: If $f(x) = x^2 - 5x - 1$, what is the value of $f(-3)$?

variants.statement: If $f(x) = x^2 - 5x - 1$, what is the value of $f(-2)$?

variants.statement: If $f(x) = x^2 - 5x - 1$, what is the value of $f(2)$?
variants.explanation: $f(2) = 1(2)^2 - 5 \cdot 2 - 1 = 4 - 10 - 1 = -7$. The sign of the middle term is where credit is usually lost.

forms.title: Exactly one solution
forms.skill: One solution means discriminant zero: k^2 = 4ac.

variants.statement: For what positive value of $k$ does the equation $x^2 + kx + 9 = 0$ have exactly one solution?
variants.explanation: Exactly one solution means the discriminant is zero: $k^2 - 4 \cdot 1 \cdot 9 = 0$, so $k^2 = 36$ and the positive root is $k = 6$.

variants.statement: For what positive value of $k$ does the equation $x^2 + kx + 256 = 0$ have exactly one solution?

forms.title: Ratios and totals

variants.statement: A drawer holds red and blue pens in the ratio $2 : 3$, and there are $20$ pens in total. How many pens are in the LARGER group?

forms.title: Outliers, mean and median
forms.skill: Outliers drag the mean; the median barely notices them.

variants.statement: A data set consists of the values $2,\ 3,\ 4,\ 5,\ 26$. If the largest value is removed, which statement is true?
options: The mean decreases by more than the median decreases.
The median decreases by more than the mean decreases.
The mean and the median decrease by the same amount.
Neither the mean nor the median changes.
variants.explanation: The outlier $26$ drags the mean up hard but barely touches the middle of the list. Removing it drops the median only from $4$ to $\frac{7}{2}$ (half a unit), while the mean falls from $8$ to $\frac{7}{2}$ — more than half a unit. Outliers hit the mean, not the median.

variants.statement: In one class of $10$ students the mean score was $60$; in another class of $5$ students it was $75$. What was the mean score of all $15$ students combined?
variants.explanation: Weight by class size: $\dfrac{10 \cdot 60 + 5 \cdot 75}{15} = \dfrac{975}{15} = 65$. Averaging the two means as $\frac{135}{2}$ ignores that the classes are different sizes.

variants.statement: In a survey, $12$ seniors and $6$ juniors preferred plan X, while $8$ seniors and $12$ juniors preferred plan Y. If a surveyed student who preferred plan X is chosen at random, what is the probability that the student is a senior?
variants.explanation: The condition shrinks the world to the $12 + 6 = 18$ students who preferred X. Among them $12$ are seniors: $\dfrac{12}{18}$. Dividing by all seniors or by everyone surveyed answers different questions.

forms.title: Area with a missing side
forms.skill: Run the area formula backwards — and keep the triangle's 1/2.

variants.statement: A rectangle has area $28$ square centimeters and width $4$ centimeters. What is its length, in centimeters?
variants.explanation: Area $=$ width $\times$ length, so the length is $\dfrac{28}{4} = 7$. Subtracting instead of dividing, or reaching for the perimeter formula, gives the traps.

forms.title: The Pythagorean theorem
forms.skill: Square, add (or subtract), then root — never add bare lengths.

variants.statement: The right triangle shown has legs of length $3$ and $4$. What is the length of its hypotenuse?
variants.explanation: By the Pythagorean theorem, $3^2 + 4^2 = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5^2$, so the hypotenuse is $5$. Adding the legs is the tempting shortcut that never works.

variants.statement: A right triangle has hypotenuse $5$ and one leg of length $3$. What is the length of the other leg?
variants.explanation: $5^2 - 3^2 = 25 - 9 = 16 = 4^2$, so the missing leg is $4$. Subtracting the lengths themselves ($5 - 3$) skips the squares.

forms.title: Equation of a circle
forms.skill: The standard form shows r^2 on the right, not r.

variants.statement: The graph of $(x + 5)^2 + (y + 4)^2 = 9$ in the $xy$-plane is a circle. What is the radius of the circle?
variants.explanation: The right side of the standard form is $r^2$, not $r$: $r^2 = 9$ gives $r = 3$. Reading $9$ off as the radius is the classic misread; the center is $(-5,\ -4)$.

forms.title: Volume, solved backwards
forms.skill: V = πr²h — divide by r squared, not by r.

variants.statement: A right circular cylinder has volume $12\pi$ cubic centimeters and base radius $2$ centimeters. What is its height, in centimeters?
variants.explanation: $V = \pi r^2 h$, so $12\pi = \pi \cdot 4 \cdot h$ and $h = \dfrac{12}{4} = 3$. Dividing by $r$ instead of $r^2$ leaves a factor of $2$ behind.

forms.title: Sine and cosine of complements
forms.skill: sin A = cos(90° − A): complementary angles trade sine for cosine.

variants.statement: In right triangle $ABC$, the right angle is at $C$ and $\sin A = \dfrac{3}{5}$. What is the value of $\cos B$?
variants.explanation: Angles $A$ and $B$ are complementary ($A + B = 90^\circ$), and the cofunction identity says $\cos B = \sin A = \dfrac{3}{5}$ — no computation needed. Solving for the third side and building $\cos B$ from scratch lands in the same place, slower.

variants.explanation: $P$ and $Q$ are complementary, so $\sin Q = \cos P = \dfrac{4}{5}$ by the cofunction identity.

forms.title: Similar triangles
forms.skill: Similarity multiplies every side by the SAME ratio — never adds.

variants.statement: Triangles $ABC$ and $DEF$ shown are similar, with $AB = 4$, $DE = 6$, and $BC = 10$. What is the length of $EF$?
variants.explanation: Similar triangles scale by one factor: $\dfrac{DE}{AB} = \dfrac{6}{4} = \frac{3}{2}$, so $EF = 10 \cdot \frac{3}{2} = 15$. Adding the same DIFFERENCE ($+2$) instead of multiplying by the same ratio gives $12$ — the additive trap.
